sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Slices and maps are the two data structures you use in virtually every Go program, and interviewers ask about them specifically because the internals are non-obvious. The slice header, append growth behaviour, and the nil map panic are all classic gotchas that distinguish a candidate who has debugged real Go code from one who has only read the spec. For freshers, this module is one of the highest-return areas to study.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Two mental models that explain the gotchas:

- **A slice is a three-field struct: (pointer to array, length, capacity).** When you pass a slice to a function, you pass this header by value — the function sees the same underlying array, but appending inside the function may create a new array if capacity is exceeded, so the caller's slice is not updated. This is why functions that grow slices must return the new slice.
- **A map is a hash table reference type — but reading a missing key is safe, writing to a nil map is not.** Unlike Python (`KeyError` on missing key), Go silently returns the zero value for a missing key. The check-existence idiom is `v, ok := m[key]`. A nil map (declared but not initialized with `make`) panics on write — always initialize maps before use.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Arrays vs slices** — arrays are fixed-length value types (`[3]int`); slices are variable-length descriptors pointing to an array (`[]int`); slices are almost always what you want
- **Slice internals: len and cap** — `len(s)` is number of elements accessible; `cap(s)` is total space in the backing array from the slice's start pointer; `s[len:cap]` is valid for reslicing
- **Append and growth** — `s = append(s, x)` adds x; if `len == cap`, Go allocates a new, larger array (typically 2x) and copies; always assign the result of `append` back
- **Slice tricks** — copy elements: `copy(dst, src)`; delete element at index i: `s = append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...)`; make a safe copy: `b := make([]T, len(a)); copy(b, a)`
- **Maps: make and literal** — `m := make(map[string]int)` or `m := map[string]int{"a": 1}`; never use a nil map for writes
- **Map iteration and nil** — map iteration order is randomized by the Go runtime (by design); `v, ok := m[key]` to check existence; writing to `var m map[string]int` (nil) panics
- **Range over slice and map** — `for i, v := range slice` gives index and copy of value; `for k, v := range m` gives key and value; use `_` to discard unwanted variable

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Append may not update the caller's slice** — `func add(s []int, v int) { s = append(s, v) }` does nothing the caller can see if a new backing array was allocated. The correct version returns the slice: `func add(s []int, v int) []int { return append(s, v) }`.
- **Writing to a nil map panics** — `var m map[string]int; m["key"] = 1` panics with 'assignment to entry in nil map'. The fix: `m := make(map[string]int)`.
- **Map iteration order is not guaranteed** — never write code that depends on maps iterating in insertion order. Go randomizes iteration intentionally to prevent accidental reliance on ordering.
- **Slice shares backing array** — `b := a[1:3]` shares the same memory as `a`. Modifying `b[0]` modifies `a[1]`. To get an independent copy: `b := make([]int, len(a)); copy(b, a)`.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"A Go slice is a three-field header — pointer, length, capacity — pointing to an underlying array. When `append` exceeds capacity, it allocates a new array, so I always assign `append` back to the original variable. Maps must be initialized with `make` before writing — a nil map panics on write but silently returns zero values on read. I use the `v, ok := m[key]` pattern to distinguish a missing key from a key with a zero value."*
